column2: For as long a time, king, as that great soul's teacher had not come, having completed the sacrifice, to his house, for that long he guarded her.
Making an incomparable and tempting form, lord of men, becoming most beautiful to see, he entered that hermitage.
He saw Vipula's body seated, motionless, with fixed eyes, as if painted in a picture.
And Ruchi, lovely-cornered of eye, with full hips and breasts, large-eyed like a lotus leaf, with a face like the full moon.
Seeing him, she suddenly wished to rise, astonished at his beauty, wishing to say "Who are you?"
Though wishing to rise, she stayed, held fast by Vipula, lord of men, and could not move.
The lord of gods spoke to her with very sweet conciliation: "Know me, pure-smiling one, to be Indra, come for your sake.
Tormented by desire born of my thought of you, satisfy me, fair-browed one; time is passing."
The sage Vipula heard Shakra speaking so, and, dwelling in his teacher's wife's body, saw the lord of the gods.
Seeing her unchanged, the lord of Shachi, ashamed, spoke again to her, bewildered by the power of yoga, O king.
Come, come, he said; then she wished to answer him, but Vipula turned that speech of the teacher's wife.
Ho, what is the purpose of your coming?: her speech, adorned with refinement, issued from her moon-like mouth.
Ashamed, she spoke that word, helpless then; and Purandara became alarmed and troubled in mind.
Noticing that change, lord of men, the thousand-eyed lord of the gods then looked with divine sight.
And he saw the sage within her body, like a reflection in a mirror, residing in the teacher's wife's body.
Seeing him joined with terrible austerity, Purandara trembled, greatly alarmed, afraid of a curse then, lord.
Leaving the teacher's wife, Vipula of great austerity entered his own body and said to the frightened Shakra:

Unmastered in senses, sinful, lustful Purandara, gods and men will not long honour you.

Hearing the great-souled Vipula's word, Shakra, ashamed and saying nothing, vanished right there.
When Shakra had gone a moment, the great ascetic Devasharman, having finished the sacrifice as he wished, came to his own hermitage.
When the teacher had come, O king, Vipula, doing what pleased him, presented the blameless wife guarded to the teacher.
Saluting his teacher, the peaceful-souled Vipula, fond of his teacher, waited upon him as before, without fear.
Then, to him rested and seated with his wife, Vipula told that deed of Shakra.
Hearing it, the mighty sage was pleased with Vipula by his conduct, austerity and discipline.
Seeing Vipula's behaviour toward his teacher, his devotion in himself and his steadiness in dharma, the lord said "Well, well."
Approving his righteous-souled pupil, devoted to dharma, he offered him a boon; and, fond of his teacher, Vipula, permitted by his teacher, practised unsurpassed austerity.
Likewise the greatly ascetic Devasharman with his wife lived fearless in a solitary forest, from the mighty slayer of Vritra.
By that deed, rivalling, lord of the earth, he roamed the earth fearless and glad, having gained fame, the best of men.
The lord also thought both worlds conquered by that deed and his great austerity, Kauravya.
Then after some time had passed, descendant of the Kurus, a gift rich in wealth and grain was made by Ruchi's sister.
At this very time some divine fair woman bearing supreme beauty went through the sky.
From her body flowers of divine fragrance fell on the ground not far from his hermitage, Bharata.
Then, king, lotus-eyed Ruchi took them, and an inviter from her relatives quickly came for her.
Her sister, dear one, the elder, named Prabhavati, was the wife of Chitraratha, lord of Anga.
Having fastened those flowers in her hair, the fair-complexioned Ruchi, invited, went to the house of the lord of Anga.
Then the great ascetic Devasharman, calling Vipula, urged him, "Go, go, for flowers," Bharata.
Without reflecting on his teacher's word, the great ascetic Vipula said "So be it," king, and went to that place.
In the place where those flowers had fallen from the sky, other unwithered flowers were also there.
Then he took those divine and lovely flowers of divine fragrance, obtained by his own austerity, Bharata.
Having got them, with glad heart, doing his teacher's word, he quickly went to Champa, garlanded with champaka.
In a solitary forest, dear one, he saw a pair of people turning like a wheel, holding each other's hands.
There one went quickly turning in the other's steps, but the other did not go so, king, and then they quarrelled.
You go fast, said one, "No," said the other; "No, no," they both said to each other, dear one.
As they vied so, this oath was made then; looking at Vipula in mind, they then spoke these words:
Whichever of us told an untruth, may that one gain the goal in the next world that belongs to the twice-born Vipula.
Hearing this, Vipula's face became downcast: "I, of such fierce austerity, and this acceptance is painful.
What sin have I done, that by this pair an unwelcome fate for all beings has been declared of me today?"
Thinking so, best of kings, Vipula with face down and head bent contemplated his own misdeed.
Then he saw six other men, with gold and silver dice, playing, joined with greed and joy.
Making that oath which was made by the pair, they too, looking at Vipula, spoke these words:
Whoever, relying on greed, dares to do wrong to us, may he gain in the next world the goal that is Vipula's.
Hearing this, Vipula did not see any mixture of dharma, Kauravya, done by himself from birth onward.
He then meditated, king, like fire placed in fire, his mind burning, having heard such a curse.
As he thought, dear one, many days and nights passed; this was in his mind: the guarding of Ruchi he had undertaken.
Having placed mark to mark and face to face, I did not tell my teacher this truth then.
This was the misdeed Vipula then took to be in himself, Kauravya, greatly fortunate one; so it was, without doubt.
Reaching the city of Champa, he gave the flowers to his teacher and duly honoured his teacher, fond of his teacher.
[Devasharman said:] "What did you see, Vipula, in that great forest? Those know you, and the wise self, and Ruchi.
[Vipula said:] "Brahmarishi, what was that pair, and who were those men, lord, who know me in truth? You ought to tell me of them."
[Devasharman said:] "That pair, Brahmana, know as day and night; it turns like a wheel; it knows your misdeed.
Those men, brahmana, who gambled with dice as if glad, know them as the seasons; they know the misdeed.
A sinful man should not trust, thinking 'No one knows me', in secret doing a sinful deed, Brahmana.
A man doing a sinful deed in secret is always seen by the seasons and by day and night as well.
Seeing you smiling with joy, not telling your teacher of the deed, they remembered, and spoke as you heard.
Day and night know, and the seasons always, the sinful or good deed in a man, of a doer of good."
[Bhishma said:] Having so spoken to Vipula, the great sage Devasharman, pleased, rejoiced, having gone to heaven with his wife and pupil.
The great sage Markandeya told me this account long ago, king, on the bank of the Ganga, between other tales.
Therefore I tell you, Partha, that in all women both are always seen: constantly good and bad.
Good women, greatly fortunate, approved, mothers of the world, support this earth with its forests and groves, king.
Bad women, ill-behaved, family-killers, of sinful resolve, are to be known by evil marks born with their bodies, king.
Thus guarding of these can be done by great souls; otherwise, tiger of kings, women cannot be guarded.
These, tiger among men, are sharp and of sharp valour; none of them has a dear one in union with men.
They are magical creatures, to be used and made, bull of the Bharatas; and they do not delight in a single man, Pandava.
Men should not have affection for them, nor jealousy, king; one should enjoy with weariness, resorting to dharma.
A man acting otherwise would be destroyed, descendant of the Kurus; in every way, tiger of kings, a method is honoured everywhere.
Women were guarded in that way by Vipula alone; no other in the world of men can guard women, king.
[Bhishma said:] This is held the most to be reflected on of all dharmas, to whom a maiden should be given, lord of the earth.
Having considered conduct, learning, family and deeds, the maiden is to be given with water to a worthy groom; this is the constant dharma of good brahmanas, Yudhishthira.
One who gives, being favourable, a bride to be brought, should so bring her; this is the eternal dharma of the good and of kshatriyas.
One who leaves aside his own wish and follows the maiden's wish, and she is given to whom she wishes, Yudhishthira: knowers of dharma call this dharma Gandharva.
Having bought with much wealth and tempted the relatives, king, the wise call this the dharma of asuras.
Carrying off by force a weeping maiden from home from her weeping family, having killed and cut heads, is the Rakshasa mark of dharma, dear one.
Of the five, three are righteous and two unrighteous, Yudhishthira; the Paishacha and Asura are never to be practised.
Brahma, Kshatra and Gandharva are righteous, bull among men; separately or mixed they are to be done, without doubt.
The brahmin wife should be the senior; for a kshatriya, a kshatriya woman; for pleasure a shudra woman may be, others say not.
The good do not praise the begetting of offspring on a shudra woman; a brahmin begetting on a shudra woman is given an expiation.
A man of thirty should marry a ten-year-old wife, unclad; or one of twenty-one a seven-year-old.
A maiden who has no brother or father, bull of the Bharatas, he should never marry, for she is a daughter appointed as son.
A maiden of age should wait three years; when the fourth comes, she should herself find a husband.
Her offspring is lost and her husband too, bull of the Bharatas; so one acting otherwise would be blamed by Prajapati.
One not of her mother's sapinda and not of her father's gotra: Manu said that one should marry such a woman.
[Yudhishthira said:] If a bride-price has been given by one and another says "I give", another speaks by force and another shows wealth,
and another is the one who takes the hand, whose is the maiden, grandfather? Be our eye as we seek the truth.
[Bhishma said:] Whatever human act is undertaken for establishment, with mantra, and has been consecrated, a falsehood in it is a sin.
Wife, husband, priest, teacher, pupil and instructor deserve punishment for lying; others say not.
Manu does not praise agreement without desire; what is false, disgraceful and unrighteous angers dharma.
There is no sole fault in one alone; that giving is not found where they give righteously and where they buy, Bharata.
Permitted by relatives, one should apply mantra and offering; so those mantras succeed, and never for one not given.
The agreement by mantra made here between wife and husband is called the weightier, and the one made by kinsmen.
The husband knows the wife given by the gods by the rule of dharma; she rejects divine or human false speech.
[Yudhishthira said:] If, when a maiden's price has been paid, a better groom comes, joined with dharma, desire and wealth, should untruth be said or not?
In that fault on both sides, doing the better, one should act. This is held the most to be reflected on of all our dharmas.
Be our eye as we seek the truth; tell all this; I am not satisfied; let it be told.
[Vyasa said:] The price is not the end-making; knowing so, one does not take it; the good never give a maiden for a price.
Kinsmen ask a price for a maiden of other qualities; one who gives, being favourable, saying "Adorn her and take her",
gives that and her too; that is not a price, nor a sale; having received it, it should be given. This is eternal dharma.
I shall give you the maiden was not said earlier; those who say it, those who do not, and those who say it as necessary,
ask each other until the taking of the hand. We have heard that the groom was formerly given the maiden by the Maruts.
A maiden is not to be given to the unwilling, so said the sages' injunction; its root, I think, is desire, the root of offspring.
Considering the many faults of living together of two who hate each other, hear how the price does not make the end.
I carried off two maidens for Vichitravirya, having conquered all the Magadhas, Kashis and Kosalas; one whose hand had been taken got a price, the other did not.
The one whose hand was taken there should be released, my father said; the Kaurava took the other maiden.
He asked of another, fearing his father's word, and my father's wish for dharma was exceedingly great.
Then I said these words, king, wishing conduct: "I wish to know conduct in truth," again and again.
When I had so spoken, my father, Bahlika, best of upholders of dharma, great king, said:

If for you the end is by price and not by taking the hand, let her who got a price wait at the throwing of parched grain on the chosen husband.

No one should do anything to her by mantra.
Chosen by herself, Savitri was accepted by her father; some praise that, the knowers of dharma, not others.
Others have not done this, nor have the good ever; but the conduct of the good is the weightier mark of dharma.
In this very matter Sukratu spoke, the grandson of the great-souled Janaka, king of Videha:

On a path practised by the bad, how could there be recitation? Question or doubt would blame this of the good.

[Bhishma said:] As the self, so the son; a daughter is equal to a son; when she stands in the self, how can another take the wealth?
What is a mother's dowry is a maiden's portion alone; or a daughter's son would take the inheritance of a childless father.

Manu, wishing to go to heaven, entrusted women to men: weak, with little clothing, friends, wishing to win by truth,

A wife is your trust, dharma, and only pleasures of love; service and refinement depend on her; let them depend on you.
For woman there is no sacrifice, no funeral rite and no fasting; her dharma is serving her husband, and by that she wins heaven.
The father protects in childhood, the husband in youth, the sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence.
These women are called Shri; one wishing prosperity should honour them; cherished and restrained, a woman becomes Shri, Bharata.
[Yudhishthira said:] I have a certain doubt; tell it to me, grandfather. In this painful calamity whom else should we ask?
As a man must act and what is eternal dharma, all this you ought to explain, mighty-armed.
Four wives are ordained for a brahmana, grandfather: brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra, if he wishes pleasure.
Among sons born there of all of them, best of the Kurus, in order, which of them deserves the paternal inheritance?
By whom and what should be taken from the father's wealth, grandfather? I wish to hear told the division among them that is remembered.
[Bhishma said:] Brahmana, kshatriya and vaishya are the three twice-born classes; among these dharma is ordained for the brahmana, Yudhishthira.
By accident or greed or desire, scorcher of foes, a shudra woman may be for a brahmana, but is not remembered as an example.
A brahmana, placing a shudra woman on his bed, becomes afflicted, and an expiation is made by the rule seen.
The marked bull, the vehicle, whatever is the chief, the son of the brahmin wife should take as one portion from the father's wealth.
The rest of the brahmin's property is to be made tenfold, Yudhishthira; of that, four shares are to be taken by him from the father's wealth.
The son of the kshatriya woman is also a brahmana, without doubt; by his mother's distinction he deserves to take three shares.
Born in the third class, of the vaishya woman, from a brahmana, he is to take two shares from the brahmin's property, Yudhishthira.
One born of a shudra woman from a brahmana is remembered as one to whom wealth is to be given always; a little is to be given to a shudra woman's son, Bharata.
This is the order of wealth divided tenfold; among those born of women of the same class, equal shares should be made.
They consider the shudra woman's son not a brahmana, from lack of skill; but one born in the three classes from a brahmana becomes a brahmana.

Non-cruelty is the highest dharma: it is given to him for that; wherever he is born, he is seen for his qualities.

while she stays, no other may do it; the brahmin wife alone should do it for the brahmana, Yudhishthira.
